title: Harnessing highly efficient coherent polariton parametric emission in quantum confined perovskite microcavities

paper_content.abstract:
Microcavity exciton polaritons emerge as a versatile platform for nonlinear optical effects thanks to the
unique dispersion which enables a manifold of energy and wavevector conserved processes. However,
efficient generation of parametric emission while preserving coherence remains challenging mainly due to
lack of strong parametric interactions compared to simultaneous interaction with relaxation channels.
Herein, we report highly efficient parametric emission with sub-1-meV linewidth from quantum confined
microcavities, enabling the first observation of strong phase coherence between the two parametric species.
Quantum size effect enabled by surface disorder in confined systems acts as the microscopic mechanism
for the observed anomalous enhancement of parametric emission, playing important role in triggering
exotic parametric interactions for microcavity polaritons. Finally, we demonstrate the emergence of
polariton supersolid phase at room temperature in a coherent parametric oscillator, characterized by periodic
density modulation in real space that indicates the breaking of translational symmetry.
paper_content.introduction:
Exciton-polaritons, hybrid light-matter quasiparticles formed through strong photon-exciton coupling,
have established themselves as a versatile platform for investigating nonlinear quantum optics and
collective coherent phenomena in driven-dissipative systems1-4. The inherent nonlinearity of these bosonic
quasi-particles, originating from the excitonic component, enables efficient polariton-polariton scattering
processes. Further enriched by the distinctive dispersion of multiple polariton bands, microcavity polariton
supports a manifold of parametric interactions that circumvent conventional phase-matching constraints,
enabling efficient parametric emission at reduced power consumption5-9. Among the various types of
parametric interactions, energy-degenerate optical parametric oscillation (OPO, or parametric scattering)9-
16 has garnered significant interest for its potential to generate phase-correlated or quantum-entangled
photon pairs17-19, given that the signal and idler states emerge from source polaritons sharing identical
quantum statistics. More recently, such an OPO configuration has attracted huge interest in the study of the
supersolid phase of matter20,21 , characterized by the formation of periodic density modulations in real
space22-26, thanks to the symmetric momentum-space distribution and the interacting nature of signal and
idler polaritons. Nevertheless, most experimental implementations of such configurations exhibit
suboptimal parametric emission efficiencies-typically characterized by low signal/idler-to-source polariton
intensity ratios-with reported enhancement often requiring pump powers few times above threshold11.
These improvements, however, are inevitably accompanied by spectral broadening, which degrades the
coherence and interaction properties of the signal and idler polaritons. This inefficiency may arise from
either insufficient nonlinear interaction strengths or rapid depletion of parametric states12,13, limiting the
intricate application of parametric interactions and highlighting the need for strategies that simultaneously
enhance emission efficiency while preserving spectral purity.

In this work, we report highly efficient and spectrally pure interbranch energy-degenerate polariton
parametric emission in quantum confined CsPbBr microcavities. Dispersion characteristics enabled by
3
surface disorder (refer to morphological roughness, in this context) and geometric confinement allow
enhanced parametric interactions. Such configuration further endows high-purity polariton states on
different branches to have phase-matched energy levels and increased density of states, thereby enabling
efficient parametric emission while preserving sub-1-meV linewidth. Benefiting from the efficient emission,
phase coherence between signal and idler polaritons in momentum space with clear visibility were observed,
showing the potential for coherent interactions into the quantum regime. With respect to the mechanism
that leads to strong parametric emission, corresponding experimental and theoretical studies reveal a
quantum size effect and highlight the crucial role of disorder in strongly confined regime. Finally, we
observed the room temperature supersolid phase utilizing the efficient coherent parametric oscillator. Our
findings reveal the crucial role of quantum confinement and disorder potential landscape in facilitating
exotic parametric interactions.

are modified on de Broglie wavelength scale and give rise to anomalously strong and coherent parametric

which are referred to as ‘signal’ and ‘idler’ polaritons, respectively.

As illustrated in Fig. 2a for a MP with L = 1.9 μm, when pumped non-resonantly (1 kHz, 100 fs, 400
y
nm) above condensation threshold, in addition to the condensate spanning the central region in angle-
resolved PL spectra, two sharp emissions corresponding to signal and idler states emerge, with intensity
rivaling that of the condensate. In the energy-degenerate interbranch parametric scattering process,
components near k = 0 would serve as the most effective source to create parametric polariton pairs at
y
opposite in-plane wavevectors, due to the highly satisfied phase matching condition5,7,40,41. Therefore, we
extracted the spectra from central region of the respective states (Supplementary Fig. 9), considering that
the source emission is broadened due to spatial confinement33. As shown in Fig. 2a right panel, strong signal
and idler emission exhibited linewidth down to ~0.78 meV, with signal emission reaching ~1.35 times the
intensity of remaining source emission. The above-unity signal-to-source ratio suggests depletion of the
source state in the stimulated regime and indicates highly efficient nonlinear parametric process, a
characteristic that has likewise been reported in pure-photonic OPOs42,43. The depletion of source state has
also been observed in intrabranch polariton OPOs in the stimulated regime44,45. In our theoretical study, an
above-unity ratio has also been observed as presented in the following discussion on quantum size effect.
An imbalance in the intensity of signal and idler emission could also be observed, which is expected in
these microcavities dressed with disorder and confinement37,46,47, considering the asymmetry in both
population and depletion pathways in the driven-dissipative system.

Furthermore, to recognize the population mechanism for nonlinear parametric emission, resonant and
non-resonant pump experiments were performed in an identical microcavity (Supplementary Fig. 10–12).
The comparable parametric ratio and intensity growth behavior suggested the dictating role of nonlinear
parametric scattering, rather than direct condensation fed by the exciton reservoir. Meanwhile, we observed
that blue shifting the source condensate via increasing pumping fluence simultaneously blueshifts the signal
and idler emissions, with their wave vectors shifting toward larger values, governed by the parabolic
dispersion of the LPB22,23 (Supplementary Fig. 13). In addition, to exclude the edge scattering effect
previously observed for the laterally confined cavities, we performed real-space-resolved spectroscopy of
a strongly confined microcavity and identified that the parametric emission solely comes from center of the
microcavity (Supplementary Fig. 14).

To estimate the parametric emission intensity and coherence, a comparison with reported values10,11,13-
16,23 was summarized and plotted in Fig. 2b, in respect of linewidth and parametric emission ratio. Our
parametric emission with intensity rivaling that of the source condensate while maintaining sub-1-meV
linewidth shows superiority as an efficient coherent polariton parametric oscillator. Such pure emission
holds promise to study coherent interactions for parametric polaritons. We use k-space interferometry as a
proof-of-concept demonstration to show its capability. Fig. 2c shows the experimental configuration: the
Michelson interference with images superimposing mirror-symmetrically were carried out in k-space, with
signal and idler polariton emission on two opposite k directions superimposed with each other. To directly
visualize the superiority of strong parametric emission with preserved coherence in quantum confinement
regime, we compare the k-space interferometry in a strongly confined microcavity and a weakly confined
cavity (both dressed with disorder) at time delay of ~0.03 ps. Fig. 2d shows the momentum space
interferogram for a strongly confined microcavity at 9 μJ cm-2 (1.5 P ) where clear interference fringes
th
were observed for overlapping signal and idler polaritons, as circled out by white dashed boxes on one side
of the Fourier plane. The visibility is calculated to be ~0.72 according to the line profile of the interference
fringes (Fig. 2e). Such visibility demonstrates strong phase coherence between signal and idler polaritons
in our microcavities. In contrast, for the weakly confined microcavity, when it was pumped at similar level
(10 μJ cm-2, 1.5 P ), parametric emission is rather weak (Supplementary Fig. 15). Therefore, higher pump
th
fluence (20 μJ cm-2, 3.0 P ) is needed for the generation of strong parametric emission comparable with
th
the strongly confined microcavities (Fig. 2f). Such pump fluence inevitably leads to dephasing processes
and broadening of the linewidth of signal and idler polaritons (Fig. 2f and g, Supplementary Fig. 16).

The role of confinement in enhancing polariton–polariton interactions can be anticipated from the
increased wavefunction overlap and thus stronger nonlinear coupling, as has been reported in a variety of
microcavity configurations36,37,39,48. However, in previously reported confined schemes13,14, the parametric
emission intensity is often not substantially improved compared to planar microcavities. In our case, the
disorder potential acts as the key enabler for the observation of strong coherent parametric emission. To
qualitatively illustrate its role, we investigated variation of parametric emission with different levels of
disorder (Supplementary Fig. 17). The markedly enhanced parametric emission in the presence of a
moderate amount of disorder highlights its crucial importance in triggering efficient parametric emission.
The disorder potential breaks overall inversion symmetry and thereby lifts the degeneracy for wavevector
selection rules36,39,49, allowing the parametric process to occur under less stringent conditions.

To further examine how confinement and disorder correlate and mediate parametric interactions, we
compiled a statistical data set with the lateral confinement size (L ) taken as the independent variable. The
y
confinement size (L ) can be accurately defined, whereas the degree of disorder is difficult to parameterize.
y
For each size, all accessible disorder configurations measured are included, effectively averaging over
random realizations and allowing the overall trends and systematic behavior to be revealed. The statistical
analysis is shown in Fig. 3 and carried out in parallel with theory based on the driven-dissipative Gross-
Pitaevskii equation as described in the Methods section. An identical trend is observed for experiments
(scatters) and theoretical results (lines) that with decreasing confinement dimension, the fluctuation in
parametric scattering ratio becomes stronger. Such phenomenon is typically observed in strongly interacting
systems such as nano-sized superconductors50-53. For small particles or thin films, trivial size variation could
lead to evident changes in number of energy levels near the Fermi energy, causing prominent fluctuations
in the spectral density and are reflected in a gradually increasing fluctuation in order parameters like
superconducting transition temperature52 or energy gap53, etc.

Adopting the scheme to our polariton OPO, we attribute such rapid fluctuation to an analogous quantum
size effect. When the system size (predominated by confinement L in CsPbBr microcavity) becomes
y 3
comparable to de Broglie wavelength32, disorder potential would induces a strong sensitivity of nonlinear
processes to system parameters like energy level position, energy level density of states, etc. In this regime,
quantization of energy and momentum becomes strong and starts playing significant roles in mediating
parametric interaction strength. Disorder in such quantum confinement configuration induce significant
fluctuations in energy positions and density of states for signal, source and idler on respective LPBs even
with small perturbations, strongly affecting the phase matching conditions and final state population density
to stimulate efficient parametric scattering. As a result, the parametric ratio becomes rapidly oscillating as
depicted by eye-guided background peaks in Fig. 3a. The fine-energy-matching mechanism could also be
reflected in the gradually decreasing energy mismatch of signal and source, idler and source with increasing
pump fluence (Supplementary Fig. 18) and acquisition of highly efficient parametric emission in strongly
confined microcavities with small mismatch (shown in Supplementary Fig. 19 in a histogram map that
correlates energy mismatch into the counted ratio).

Disorder is present in all cavities, but its impact becomes most pronounced when confinement approaches
dimension comparable to the polariton de Broglie wavelength. To quantify the fluctuations and accessible
ratios across confinement regimes, we select two confinement ranges (1.8–3.6 μm, and 10.8–12.6 μm) and
plot the corresponding fluctuation level in probability histogram. For strongly confined regime (upper
panel), the histogram distributes in a broad ‘ratio’ range and exhibits a probability amplitude that decreases
with larger ‘ratio’. However, in weakly confined systems (lower panel), such histogram mainly distributes
in a small ‘ratio’ range on the lower value side. Although the distribution shown in Fig. 3a and b refers to
the randomness in emission intensity, a statistical analysis on its maximum and average value is meaningful
in finding the expectation values in obtaining an efficient parametric oscillator, as shown in Fig. 3c. An
increasing trend is observed for both maximum (red) and average (blue) values in scattering efficiency
when decreasing confinement, indicating that the role of disorder is fully revealed in the strongly confined
regime.

The coherent interacting nature, combined with conjugated k-space position of the parametric polaritons
makes energy-degenerate OPO an ideal platform to investigate crystallized supersolid phase of the quantum
fluid of light. The recently observed supersolidity of polariton OPO in GaAs at liquid helium temperature
is a crucial step towards this goal22,23. Benefitting from the large exciton binding energy and robust light-
matter interaction of CsPbBr at room temperature27,29,30,34,54,55, we realize such supersolidity at ambient
3
conditions, substantiated by the observation of two thresholds in parametric emission growth behavior, and
coordinate space pattern formation with a period correlated with k position of the parametric polariton.
As illustrated in Fig. 4a, the evolution of intensity exhibits two nonlinear thresholds (marked by black dashed
lines), with sub-linear growth at low pump fluence and subsequent nonlinear growth of source (5.35 μJ cm-
2) and signal/idler (7.44 μJ cm-2), respectively. Different growth behavior of parametric emission with
respect to source BEC density (I) is retrieved by examining the respective intensity evolution closely near
the two thresholds, as shown in Fig. 4b and denoted by I, I0.25, and I0.9. Below the first threshold, incoherent
relaxation from the exciton reservoir, and linear scattering from source polariton is responsible for the
population at signal and idler states. Crossing the first threshold, source condensate first exhibits nonlinear
growth. With source condensate population building up, nonlinear parametric scattering was initiated and
nonlinearly increases the signal and idler intensity, accompanied by a dramatic reorganization in momentum
space as shown in the insets of Fig. 4b. The left inset depicts a uniform exciton reservoir distribution, while
the right inset highlights coherent parametric scattering between the source condensate and conjugate
signal/idler polaritons. Respective angle-resolved PL spectra and momentum space images for this
microcavity at different pump fluences are depicted in Supplementary Fig. 20.

As shown in Fig. 4c–f, for two parametric oscillators with angle-resolved PL spectra (Fig. 4c and e)
showing signal and idler polaritons centered at distinct wavevectors (8.0 μm-1 and 7.2 μm-1), corresponding
features were observed in real space emission patterns. The real space images (Fig. 4d and f, upper panels)
with striking periodic fringes confirm a ‘lattice’ constant of 0.78 μm and 0.87 μm by extracting the line
profiles (lower panels). Such spatial periodicity aligns precisely with the momentum-space emission peaks
via Fourier reciprocity, confirming the spontaneous ‘crystallization’ of the polariton condensate and its
supersolid nature. We believe that such coherent parametric emission with intensity comparable to source
condensate enables direct observation of an anomalous supersolid phase with periodic stripes in real space,
which would otherwise be obscured by strong source condensate emission. In strongly confined
microcavities, such phenomenon with correlated momentum space position and real space fringe spacing
was also observed (Supplementary Fig. 21), except with presence of limited number of fringes due to the
finite dimensionality. Circumventing the extreme cooling requirements of traditional quantum fluids
establishes the optical parametric oscillator in our microcavity as an ideal testbed for emergent macroscopic
quantum effects.

In summary, this work establishes quantum confined semiconductor microcavities as a robust platform for
strong coherent parametric polariton generation through the synergistic interplay of geometric confinement
and surface disorder. Highly efficient parametric emission is achieved in presence of disorder in the strongly
confined regime, with parametric emission intensity rivaling those of the source condensate, while
preserving high spectra-purity with sub-1-meV linewidth. The ultra-narrowband emission enables the
observation of phase coherence between signal and idler polaritons. Statistical analysis from experiments
and theory reveals the role of quantum size effect in mediating parametric emission intensity in the quantum
confined microcavity. In addition, the efficient emission enables direct observation of emerging supersolid
phase at room temperature. These results demonstrate that non-trivial potential landscape act as key
enablers of unconventional parametric phenomena—which could be readily extended to other material
platforms, providing transformation strategies to harness polariton nonlinearities and accelerate the
development of quantum photonic devices.

Perovskite Synthesis
The CsPbBr microplatelets were synthesized using an anti-solvent method31. CsBr and PbBr powders of
3 2
analytical grade were mixed in a 1:1 molar ratio and dissolved in dimethylformamide to prepare a 20 mM
precursor solution. Glass substrates were placed in a placed in dichloromethane anti-solvent filled beaker,
and the precursor solution was dropped onto the substrates, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 2a. Beaker was
covered with perforated Parafilm to and placed in an oven with temperature of 30 ℃ for 48 h, enabling
evaporation and CsPbBr single crystal growth. The synthesis procedure yields microplatelets of various
3
lateral dimensions, shown in Supplementary Fig. 2b.

Microcavity Fabrication
The CsPbBr microcavity consists of top and bottom distributed Bragg reflector (DBR) mirrors and the
3
central CsPbBr microplatelets. Bottom DBR consists of 20 pairs of electron-beam evaporated titanium
3
oxide (TiO ) and silicon dioxide (SiO ) with quarter-wavelength thickness, and top DBR consists of 8 pairs
2 2
of such oxide layers. CsPbBr microplatelets were dry transferred to bottom DBR with
3
polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) stamps, followed by ~60 nm PMMA layer encapsulation before top mirror
evaporation, acting as protection layer for perovskites.

Optical Characterization
Optical characterization was conducted using a custom-built system based on Fourier imaging, allowing
for both real-space and momentum-space resolved spectroscopy and imaging. For real space imaging and
spectroscopy on the micron-scale sized sample, a short-focal length lens was used to magnify the image, to
resolve emission from the microplatelet microcavity. A Michelson interferometer with mirror symmetric
configuration was utilized to investigate first-order spatial and temporal coherence in both real space and
k-space. Pump laser spot size was enlarged by a long focal distance lens in the excitation path, as shown in
Supplementary Fig. 6. Emission from the sample was captured with a 100× objective (NA = 0.9) and
spatially filtered with an adjustable rectangular aperture at the focal plane and directed to a liquid nitrogen-
cooled charge-coupled device (CCD) spectrometer (Princeton Instruments, SP-2500i). For pulsed
excitation, the 800 nm fundamental pulses (100 fs, 1 kHz) from a Coherent Astrella regenerative amplifier
were directed to a beta barium borate (BBO) crystal to generate non-resonant pump pulses at 400 nm, or
directed to an optical parametric amplifier (Coherent OperA Solo) to generate resonant pump pulses at 540
nm. Continuous-wave excitation was performed using a 405 nm laser.

Other characterizations
Atomic force microscopy (AFM) imaging was carried out in tapping mode with a BRUKER Dimension
ICON system, while laser confocal microscopy was performed using a Zeiss LSM800 Airyscan confocal
microscope. X-Ray diffraction (XRD) measurement was performed with Rigaku XtaLAB PRO. Annular
dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) characterization was performed with Titan
Cubed Themis G2 at 300 kV voltage. SEM images were obtained from Thermo Fisher Helios G4 UX
DualBeam system.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript by Deng et al. reports efficient parametric emission from CsPbBr3 microcavities while preserving a sub 1meV linewidth. The authors claim that the mechanism enabling the highly efficient generation of parametric emission is modulated by quantum confinement. Furthermore, the authors observe spontaneous ‘crystallization’ at room temperature forming a supersolid phase with real space periodicity. The work is relevant to the community, the efficient generation of narrow linewidth parametric emission is a remarkable outcome. However, a deeper analysis of the mechanism enabling this process is essential to make this a scalable process.
Main Comments:
1) The manuscript attributes the discretization of the polariton dispersion to a combination of geometric confinement and disordered surface potentials, with a reported 7.5 meV mode spacing. However, the discussion does not clearly distinguish the contributions from in-plane confinement and disorder. A systematic study isolating the effects of in-plane confinement, and surface roughness, such as comparing dispersions for different lateral sizes and controlled disorder amplitudes, would strengthen the mechanistic interpretation and clarify the origin of the observed discretization. From Fig. 1b, the roughness reaches ~10 nm, an analysis showing that this amplitude can localize lower polaritons and yield a level spacing on the order of the observed, would be beneficial. To separate the two contributions, k-space reflectance for similar cavities with reduced surface roughness would explain how the spacing and the appearance of discrete lines evolve relative to surface roughness.
2) The term “non-confined cavity” needs an explicit definition. A more detailed explanation of what this means would benefit the paper. Does this denote a planar microcavity with a larger crystal? The authors should report the fabrication process for this larger device. Providing these details will allow for a fair comparison with the confined structures.
3) The authors claim that the disordered surface potentials that are formed as a result of the fabrication process are instrumental in generating fine modes and efficient parametric emission. However, the role of the disorder in enhancing parametric emission if not quantitively measured. A study of how the different levels of surface roughness effect the signal /ideler ratio would be beneficial.
4) The authors chose CsPbBr₃ as the active material, but the manuscript does not justify why this particular halide perovskite is uniquely suited for sustaining parametric scattering and supersolid behavior. Could other halide compositions (e.g., CsPbI₃, mixed halides, or hybrid organic-inorganics) offer advantages in terms of exciton binding energy, linewidth, or tunability of the cavity modes? A few sentences in the introduction would help here.
5) The manuscript would benefit from structural characterization of the CsPbBr₃ microplatelets. While the microcavities are strongly characterized, no direct evidence is provided for the crystallographic quality or phase purity of the material. Techniques such as X-ray diffraction could confirm the absence of secondary phases, strain, or structural defects that might influence the dispersion and parametric scattering behavior. Including such data would strengthen the link between the observed effects in the strongly coupled system and the intrinsic properties of the active material, and ensure that the reported effects are not influenced by variations in material quality.
6) Given that perovskites are prone to point defects and surface traps, how do the authors ensure that these do not dominate the coherence and linewidth of the parametric emission? Is there any passivation strategy or post-treatment applied or can you comments on how that might affect properties?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The manuscript “Harnessing highly efficient coherent polariton parametric emission in quantum confined perovskite microcavities” by Xinyi Deng et al. reports the first-time observation of resonantly enhanced parametric scattering of exciton- polaritons in a halide perovskite microcavity. The authors emphasize the key result of their work: the strong influence of in- plane polariton quantization, accompanied by potential disorder, on the nonlinear optical response of the studied system. They experimentally observe coherent polariton emission involving parametric scattering and also claim the “first observation of strong phase coherence between the two parametric species in momentum space.”
The importance of the observations is not in doubt: the suggested arrangement is suitable for generating phase-correlated photon pairs, with potential for operation down to the single-photon regime. The halide perovskite platform is favorable in this sense, as it is known for its ultimate quantum efficiency of exciton-enabled light emission.
The manuscript is generally well-written. However, some further clarifications and polishing of the text would be beneficial, as noted below. The team employs well-established experimental methods; therefore, the data quality is suitable. The analytical model is clear; some parameters used need to be specified in the updated version of the manuscript.
Although I am generally positive about this work, I must point out that some of the authors’ claims require further justification. The authors have to address several questions before I can recommend this work for publication in Nature Communications.
Major issue:
My primary concern is related to the mechanisms of population of signal and idler states. I can suggest at least three of those:
(1) Conventional relaxation from the reservoir to a resonant state (gain).
(2) Linear scattering of polaritons from the source to signal and idler states.
(3) Nonlinear parametric scattering of source polaritons towards signal/idler state, claimed as the primary mechanism.
Firstly, the right panel in Figure 2a clearly shows the strong asymmetry in signal (1.36)/idler (0.43) relative intensities. In case of mechanism (3), exclusively responsible signal/idler population, this picture must be purely symmetric. The largest of these two values is compared to other works in Figure 2b and is referred to as “parametric emission efficiency”, which might mislead the reader. This efficiency is fundamentally limited by the minimum of the two values mentioned for each particular measurement.
The authors state in the text: ”Below the first threshold, incoherent relaxation from the exciton reservoir is responsible for the population at signal and idler states.” It is unclear why authors neglect this mechanism when discussing the system behavior above the first thresholds.
Let me suggest an explanation of the observed effects involving only mechanisms (1) and (2). Above the first threshold, the condensate appears at the source state. The polaritons there undergo elastic scattering into signal/idler modes, with efficiency enhanced by surface disorder. These scattered polaritons seed the condensates in signal/idler states, which appear at a larger threshold and remain coherent with the source, as they are seeded by polaritons coming from it. Another reason for the signal, source, and idler states to be mutually coherent is the complete overlap of these modes in real space.
The condensation threshold for the signal/idler states can be larger than that of the source state for several reasons, including differences in polariton lifetimes. The nearest polaritonic state below the source is more than 50 meV apart, while for signal/idler states, this distance is below 10 meV.
I firmly believe that with this massive amount of experimental data in hand, authors can distinguish between mechanisms (1- 3) more accurately.

To distinguish pump photons from those in a condensate (and estimate the condensate emission rate), one can pump at an angle, staying within the positive/negative in-plane wavevectors, yet remaining resonant with the source mode.

Figure S5 (d-f) - is it a single frequency or summation over a range?

Figure S7 (g) instead of (b). It is unclear why the source and idler energy- and wavevector-dependent spectra are plotted on different axes. I suggest using the exact representation and adding the signal plots as well.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
The work by Deng et al. reports on the efficient generation of parametric emission in a polaritonic microcavity. The authors claim that the presence of random in-plane potentials is responsible for the observed anomalous enhancement of parametric scattering. To support their claims, they first present a comparison among three configurations: a non-confined microcavity (showing low-efficiency scattering), a laterally confined cavity without random potential (showing no parametric scattering), and a laterally confined cavity with random potential (exhibiting highly efficient scattering). They then perform statistical analysis to justify the observed high efficiency and develop a theoretical model. Finally, they also present evidence of supersolidity at room temperature.
The topic is certainly interesting, and the overall idea of investigating the role of disorder and lateral confinement in the regime of nonlinear polariton scattering is nice. However, I found some aspects of the work problematic and the final claims somewhat unclear. The authors attempt to highlight the role of disorder, suggesting that scattering is not observed in a similar laterally confined structure without disorder. This implies that disorder is a fundamental requirement. However, a close examination of Fig. S9 clearly shows that phase matching cannot be satisfied in that case. Therefore, the comparison is not accurate, and the authors’ claim appears incorrect, especially considering that parametric scattering has been previously observed in laterally confined systems (e.g., 10.1103/PhysRevB.87.155302). Indeed, they later acknowledge that downscaling the lateral confinement introduces randomness in the phase-matching conditions, leading to larger fluctuations in the occurrence of highly efficient parametric emission. However, it is unclear what the authors are precisely claiming here. If they intend to argue that strong and coherent parametric emission is uniquely associated with laterally confined disordered microcavities, then they should present a reference sample—free from disorder but with well-matched phase-matching conditions—for a meaningful comparison. Otherwise, the role of disorder appears to be limited to mode broadening which facilitate phase matching, which is less significant.
Even the comparison with the non-confined system is problematic. The sample shown in Fig. S8 exhibits a more positive detuning (with visible lasing around 2323 meV), while the confined-disordered cavity is more negatively detuned (~2300 meV). This results in a higher excitonic fraction for the non-confined sample, which strongly influences both the visibility of the parametric emission and, in fact, the condensate itself. The condensate at k=0 in the non-confined sample appears to have lower visibility compared to that of the confined-disordered cavity. Therefore, this comparison does not convincingly support the claims regarding coherence. Moreover, the reported efficiency value—while I appreciate the large statistical analysis and the effort put into developing a suitable model—also appears problematic. The claimed efficiency seems to exceed the theoretical limit for a parametric process, in which the combined intensity of the signal and idler cannot surpass that of the pump. This suggests that there may be an issue in how the overall intensity of the condensate is being evaluated.
Overall, although the work has potential, I cannot recommend publication of the manuscript in its current form. A clear and convincing demonstration of the key claims—particularly regarding the role of disorder and the reported efficiency—is necessary before the work can be considered for publication.
Below is a list of my comments.
-In the introduction, the authors cite the work from J. Wu et al. (10.1021/acs.nanolett.1c00283), stating that the reported case exhibits suboptimal parametric emission efficiency and that pump powers "several times" above the condensation threshold are required to observe parametric scattering. However, upon reviewing the referenced paper, it is clear that parametric scattering is already visible at pump powers 2–3 times above the condensation threshold. This would more accurately be described as "a few times," rather than "several," and does not support the implication of particularly poor efficiency.
-The authors used the same sample in one of their recent publications to observe polariton condensation under CW excitation. Why a pulsed excitation scheme was chosen for the present experiments?. Could the authors show how the excitation regime (CW vs. pulsed) influences the key observed properties—such as parametric efficiency, linewidth, and coherence? Are these parameters intrinsic to the system or strongly dependent on the excitation conditions?
-Still regarding the excitation scheme, polariton parametric scattering has been extensively studied in GaAs-based 1D microcavities, where, under resonant excitation, compelling evidence for phase matching and its critical role in the scattering process has been demonstrated (10.1103/PhysRevB.87.155302, 10.1002/pssb.201100115). Have the authors attempted similar measurements under resonant excitation? Would the reported effects—particularly the claimed high efficiency and coherence—still hold under pulser or CW resonant excitation? These experiments would help to establish the generality and robustness of the observed phenomena.
-Regarding the surface-smooth sample shown in Fig. S9, it is unclear why the discretization of the TE₁ and TM₁ modes is not visible. Given that this sample is used as a key comparison point, the absence of clear mode discretization raises questions about the confinement quality. As mentioned earlier, to convincingly support their claims about the role of disorder, the authors should identify a surface-smooth sample with good phase matching, similar lateral dimensions, and comparable detuning.
-How are the overall intensities of the signal, idler, and source evaluated? Part of the condensate signal may propagate outside the excitation region and thus be excluded from the intensity measurement. If so, this could lead to an underestimation of the total condensate power and therefore to high efficiency. Additionally, the authors should provide an estimate of the experimental uncertainty associated with the efficiency ratio evaluation.
-The authors emphasize that the presented configuration enables the generation of balanced signal and idler beams. However, in Fig. 2a, the idler appears to be approximately three times weaker than the signal. The authors should clarify the origin of the imbalance.
-For the non-confined microcavities below threshold dispersion should be shown.

The manuscript “Harnessing highly efficient coherent polariton parametric emission in
quantum confined perovskite microcavities” by Xinyi Deng et al. reports the first-time
observation of resonantly enhanced parametric scattering of exciton-polaritons in a
halide perovskite microcavity. The authors emphasize the key result of their work: the
strong influence of lateral polariton quantization, accompanied by potential disorder,
on the nonlinear optical response of the studied system. They experimentally observe
coherent polariton emission involving parametric scattering and also claim the “first
observation of strong phase coherence between the two parametric species in
momentum space.”
The importance of the observations is not in doubt: the suggested arrangement is
suitable for generating phase-correlated photon pairs, with potential for operation down
to the single-photon regime. The halide perovskite platform is favorable in this sense,
as it is known for its ultimate quantum efficiency of exciton-enabled light emission.

polishing of the text would be beneficial, as noted below. The team employs well-
established experimental methods; therefore, the data quality is suitable. The analytical
model is clear; some parameters used need to be specified in the updated version of the
manuscript.
Although I am generally positive about this work, I must point out that some of the
authors’ claims require further justification. The authors have to address several
questions before I can recommend this work for publication in Nature Communications.

Comment 1:
My primary concern is related to the mechanisms of population of signal and idler states.
I can suggest at least three of those:
(1) Conventional relaxation from the reservoir to a resonant state (gain).
(2) Linear scattering of polaritons from the source to signal and idler states. (power
dependence transition) not purely linear scattering.
(3) Nonlinear parametric scattering of source polaritons towards signal/idler state,
claimed as the primary mechanism.
Firstly, the right panel in Fig. 2a clearly shows the strong asymmetry in signal
(1.36)/idler (0.43) relative intensities. In case of mechanism (3), exclusively responsible
signal/idler population, this picture must be purely symmetric. The largest of these two
values is compared to other works in Fig. 2b and is referred to as “parametric emission
efficiency”, which might mislead the reader. This efficiency is fundamentally limited
by the minimum of the two values mentioned for each particular measurement.
The authors state in the text: ” Below the first threshold, incoherent relaxation from the
exciton reservoir is responsible for the population at signal and idler states.” It is unclear
why authors neglect this mechanism when discussing the system behavior above the
first thresholds.
Let me suggest an explanation of the observed effects involving only mechanisms (1)
and (2). Above the first threshold, the condensate appears at the source state. The
polaritons there undergo elastic scattering into signal/idler modes, with efficiency
enhanced by surface disorder. These scattered polaritons seed the condensates in
signal/idler states, which appear at a larger threshold and remain coherent with the
source, as they are seeded by polaritons coming from it. Another reason for the signal,
source, and idler states to be mutually coherent is the complete overlap of these modes
in real space.
The condensation threshold for the signal/idler states can be larger than that of the
source state for several reasons, including differences in polariton lifetimes. The nearest
polaritonic state below the source is more than 50 meV apart, while for signal/idler
states, this distance is below 10 meV.
I firmly believe that with this massive amount of experimental data in hand, authors
can distinguish between mechanisms (1-3) more accurately.
Another way to completely exclude the mechanism (1) from the list is to perform
additional measurements with the resonant pumping of the source state by appropriately
tuning the excitation photon energy and adjusting the spot size to avoid direct excitation
of signal/idler modes. To distinguish pump photons from those in a condensate (and
estimate the condensate emission rate), one can pump at an angle, staying within the
positive/negative lateral wavevectors, yet remaining resonant with the source mode.
Response 1.1: Signal and idler population mechanisms
We thank the reviewer for the comprehensive analysis of the possible signal and idler
population mechanisms. We performed respective experimental and theoretical
analysis, from which we attribute the nonlinear coherent signal and idler emission to
the nonlinear parametric scattering from source condensate.
According to your suggestion, we performed resonant/non-resonant pumping
experiments for an identical sample and analyzed the intensity evolution behavior. For
non-resonant pumping, a 400 nm (1 kHz, 100 fs) pulsed laser is directed onto the sample.
For resonant pumping, a 540 nm (1 kHz, 100 fs) pulsed laser is utilized and filtered to
have the laser energy slightly blue-detuned from the source condensate, while also
avoiding excitation of the exciton reservoir. The schematic of resonant pumping can be
found in Fig. S10 in the revised version of manuscript.
As shown in Fig. R5a, under non-resonant pumping conditions, the population on both
LPB1 and LPB2 emerges in the linear regime, with discretized energy levels arising
from confinement and disorder. Above the nonlinear parametric emission threshold
(Fig. R5b, the second threshold), the signal and idler emerge at energy positions
resonant with the source condensate. Fig. R5d depicts the angle-resolved PL spectra at
resonant pump condition below the nonlinear parametric scattering threshold (laser
position circled out). The emergence of a flat narrow emission, highlighted by white
arrows and just below the excitation energy, is the source emission. While at this stage,
the emission on the LPB2 at the respective energy position is missing. As the power
further increased to higher pump fluence (Fig. R5e), parametric emission appears at the
LPB2 dispersion positions resonant with source condensate. Fig. R5c and f depict the
respective growth rate of signal/idler intensity with respect to source emission intensity
under non-resonant and resonant pump conditions, respectively. The non-resonantly
pumped case features a two-threshold behavior, while resonantly pumped case exhibits
a single-threshold behavior.

The population mechanism (1)(2)(3) as raised by the reviewer stem from different
microscopic origins, therefore exhibit different efficiencies and growth behavior for the
signal/idler states with respect to source polariton. Next, we analyze in detail to assign
predominant mechanism in nonlinear regime to the nonlinear parametric scattering.
(1) Conventional relaxation from the reservoir to a resonant state:
Such possibility could be excluded with observation of nonlinear parametric emission
in resonant pump condition, where exciton reservoir is absent.
(1) + (2): Linear scattering of polaritons from the source to signal and idler states, and
seeded the nonlinear emission
We agree with the review that the mechansim (1)+(2) could generate strong signal/idler
emission. To explore, we have carefully checked experimental data. The seeding effect,
descried in this mechanism, would establish the source, signal and idler as independent
species in the nonlinear regime, being continuously replenished by the exciton reservoir.
However, the correlated evolution of the source, signal and idler modes, as reflected in
their comparable blueshift and spectral broadening (Fig. S18), indicates that these
polaritons are subject to strong mutual nonlinear interactions (Nature 639, 337–341
(2025)).
Furthermore, our observations show that forming a macroscopic occupation directly at
a high-k state on a strongly red-detuned LPB (>110 meV) requires a pump fluence of
typically 100–200 μJ·cm-2, corresponding to a high photoexcited exciton density (Sci.
Adv. 7, eabj7667 (2021)). Such high threshold is expected since LPB has its energy
minimum at k~0, and such minimum is thermo-dynamically favored than a high-k state.
Under non‑resonant pumping the polaritons preferentially relax and redistributes
population toward lower‑energy, lower‑k states—so a macroscopic occupation at a
high‑k point is hard to sustain unless the injection rate is very high (Rev. Mod. Phys. 82,
1489–1537 (2010); Phys. Rev. B 62, R2283–R2286 (2000); Phys. Rev. B 88, 121303
(2013)) or with band-structure engineered to tailor local energy minimum positions
(Nat. Commun. 4, 1749 (2013); Nat. Phys. 7, 681–686 (2011)). Consequently, the small
separation between our two thresholds (7.1 μJ·cm-2 versus 10.3 μJ·cm-2 in Fig. R5c),
would not support the hypothesis of ‘linearly scattered polariton after the first threshold
seed the nonlinear parametric scattering’, since such seeding would be far too small to
bridge the carrier density discrepancy required for a direct high-k condensate.
Finally, we attributed the mechanism that leads to nonlinear signal/idler emission as
nonlinear scattering from source polariton. As evidenced by the comparable
parametric emission ratio (Fig. R5b and e), and the respective growth rate (Fig. R5c
and f), suggesting that identical mechanism dominated such processes. The effective
slope (k ~ 1.61) in resonant case is slightly larger than that under non-resonant (k ~ 1.32)
excitation, due to a relatively stronger nonlinearity when the source condensate is quasi-
directly fed by the fs-laser pulses (Nat Commun 10, 3869 (2019)).
According to your suggestion, we have emphasized the identification of mechanism (3)
in nonlinear regime and the role of mechanism of (1) and (2) in respective regimes in
the revised version of manuscript.

Response 1.4: Mechanism for imbalance behavior.
The unbalanced intensity of signal and idler is induced by asymmetry in both population
and depletion pathways in the driven-dissipative system, which are further magnified
in presence of surface disorder that breaks inversion symmetry. Such imbalance
existing even in the nonlinear regime has been theoretically discussed (Phys. Rev. B 93,
064203 (2016)) and experimentally observed in polariton nonlinear emission
modulated by trap or disorder (Phys. Rev. Lett. 104, 126403 (2010), Nat. Commun. 13,
3080 (2022)). The emission intensity reflects averaged gain and loss at signal/idler in
the driven dissipative unequilibrium system. Exciton relaxation and scattering from the
source populate the signal and idler states, whereas radiative recombination and
relaxation into LPB2 lower energy states act as loss channels. Due to broken inversion
symmetry, the energy levels and scattering pathways become intrinsically asymmetric,
which distort these linear processes and bias the subsequently stimulated scattering and
population in nonlinear regime, resulting in the asymmetric/imbalanced angular
emission as we observed.

Response to Reviewer 4
The work by Deng et al. reports on the efficient generation of parametric emission in a
polaritonic microcavity. The authors claim that the presence of random lateral
potentials is responsible for the observed anomalous enhancement of parametric
scattering. To support their claims, they first present a comparison among three
configurations: a non-confined microcavity (showing low-efficiency scattering), a
laterally confined cavity without random potential (showing no parametric scattering),
and a laterally confined cavity with random potential (exhibiting highly efficient
scattering). They then perform statistical analysis to justify the observed high efficiency
and develop a theoretical model. Finally, they also present evidence of supersolidity at
room temperature.
The topic is certainly interesting, and the overall idea of investigating the role of
disorder and lateral confinement in the regime of nonlinear polariton scattering is nice.
However, I found some aspects of the work problematic and the final claims somewhat
unclear. Overall, although the work has potential, I cannot recommend publication of
the manuscript in its current form. A clear and convincing demonstration of the key
claims—particularly regarding the role of disorder and the reported efficiency—is
necessary before the work can be considered for publication.

We thank the reviewer for reviewing our manuscript and appreciate the reviewer’s

Comment 1.1:
The authors attempt to highlight the role of disorder, suggesting that scattering is not
observed in a similar laterally confined structure without disorder. This implies that
disorder is a fundamental requirement. However, a close examination of Fig. S9 clearly
shows that phase matching cannot be satisfied in that case. Therefore, the comparison
is not accurate, and the authors’ claim appears incorrect, especially considering that
parametric scattering has been previously observed in laterally confined systems (e.g.,
10.1103/PhysRevB.87.155302). Indeed, they later acknowledge that downscaling the
lateral confinement introduces randomness in the phase-matching conditions, leading
to larger fluctuations in the occurrence of highly efficient parametric emission.
However, it is unclear what the authors are precisely claiming here. If they intend to
argue that strong and coherent parametric emission is uniquely associated with laterally
confined disordered microcavities, then they should present a reference sample—free
from disorder but with well-matched phase-matching conditions—for a meaningful
comparison. Otherwise, the role of disorder appears to be limited to mode broadening
which facilitate phase matching, which is less significant.

## Abstract

Microcavity exciton polaritons emerge as a versatile platform for nonlinear optical effects thanks to the
unique dispersion which enables a manifold of energy and wavevector conserved processes. However,
efficient generation of parametric emission while preserving coherence remains challenging mainly due to
lack of strong parametric interactions compared to simultaneous interaction with relaxation channels.
Herein, we report highly efficient parametric emission with sub-1-meV linewidth from quantum confined
microcavities, enabling the first observation of strong phase coherence between the two parametric species.
Quantum size effect enabled by surface disorder in confined systems acts as the microscopic mechanism
for the observed anomalous enhancement of parametric emission, playing important role in triggering
exotic parametric interactions for microcavity polaritons. Finally, we demonstrate the emergence of
polariton supersolid phase at room temperature in a coherent parametric oscillator, characterized by periodic
density modulation in real space that indicates the breaking of translational symmetry.

---

## Introduction

Exciton-polaritons, hybrid light-matter quasiparticles formed through strong photon-exciton coupling,
have established themselves as a versatile platform for investigating nonlinear quantum optics and
collective coherent phenomena in driven-dissipative systems1-4. The inherent nonlinearity of these bosonic
quasi-particles, originating from the excitonic component, enables efficient polariton-polariton scattering
processes. Further enriched by the distinctive dispersion of multiple polariton bands, microcavity polariton
supports a manifold of parametric interactions that circumvent conventional phase-matching constraints,
enabling efficient parametric emission at reduced power consumption5-9. Among the various types of
parametric interactions, energy-degenerate optical parametric oscillation (OPO, or parametric scattering)9-
16 has garnered significant interest for its potential to generate phase-correlated or quantum-entangled
photon pairs17-19, given that the signal and idler states emerge from source polaritons sharing identical
quantum statistics. More recently, such an OPO configuration has attracted huge interest in the study of the
supersolid phase of matter20,21 , characterized by the formation of periodic density modulations in real
space22-26, thanks to the symmetric momentum-space distribution and the interacting nature of signal and
idler polaritons. Nevertheless, most experimental implementations of such configurations exhibit
suboptimal parametric emission efficiencies-typically characterized by low signal/idler-to-source polariton
intensity ratios-with reported enhancement often requiring pump powers few times above threshold11.
These improvements, however, are inevitably accompanied by spectral broadening, which degrades the
coherence and interaction properties of the signal and idler polaritons. This inefficiency may arise from
either insufficient nonlinear interaction strengths or rapid depletion of parametric states12,13, limiting the
intricate application of parametric interactions and highlighting the need for strategies that simultaneously
enhance emission efficiency while preserving spectral purity.

In this work, we report highly efficient and spectrally pure interbranch energy-degenerate polariton
parametric emission in quantum confined CsPbBr microcavities. Dispersion characteristics enabled by
3
surface disorder (refer to morphological roughness, in this context) and geometric confinement allow
enhanced parametric interactions. Such configuration further endows high-purity polariton states on
different branches to have phase-matched energy levels and increased density of states, thereby enabling
efficient parametric emission while preserving sub-1-meV linewidth. Benefiting from the efficient emission,
phase coherence between signal and idler polaritons in momentum space with clear visibility were observed,
showing the potential for coherent interactions into the quantum regime. With respect to the mechanism
that leads to strong parametric emission, corresponding experimental and theoretical studies reveal a
quantum size effect and highlight the crucial role of disorder in strongly confined regime. Finally, we
observed the room temperature supersolid phase utilizing the efficient coherent parametric oscillator. Our
findings reveal the crucial role of quantum confinement and disorder potential landscape in facilitating
exotic parametric interactions.

with small perturbations, strongly affecting the phase matching conditions and final state population density
to stimulate efficient parametric scattering. As a result, the parametric ratio becomes rapidly oscillating as
depicted by eye-guided background peaks in Fig. 3a. The fine-energy-matching mechanism could also be
reflected in the gradually decreasing energy mismatch of signal and source, idler and source with increasing
pump fluence (Supplementary Fig. 18) and acquisition of highly efficient parametric emission in strongly
confined microcavities with small mismatch (shown in Supplementary Fig. 19 in a histogram map that
correlates energy mismatch into the counted ratio).

Disorder is present in all cavities, but its impact becomes most pronounced when confinement approaches
dimension comparable to the polariton de Broglie wavelength. To quantify the fluctuations and accessible
ratios across confinement regimes, we select two confinement ranges (1.8–3.6 μm, and 10.8–12.6 μm) and
plot the corresponding fluctuation level in probability histogram. For strongly confined regime (upper
panel), the histogram distributes in a broad ‘ratio’ range and exhibits a probability amplitude that decreases
with larger ‘ratio’. However, in weakly confined systems (lower panel), such histogram mainly distributes
in a small ‘ratio’ range on the lower value side. Although the distribution shown in Fig. 3a and b refers to
the randomness in emission intensity, a statistical analysis on its maximum and average value is meaningful
in finding the expectation values in obtaining an efficient parametric oscillator, as shown in Fig. 3c. An
increasing trend is observed for both maximum (red) and average (blue) values in scattering efficiency
when decreasing confinement, indicating that the role of disorder is fully revealed in the strongly confined
regime.

The coherent interacting nature, combined with conjugated k-space position of the parametric polaritons
makes energy-degenerate OPO an ideal platform to investigate crystallized supersolid phase of the quantum
fluid of light. The recently observed supersolidity of polariton OPO in GaAs at liquid helium temperature
is a crucial step towards this goal22,23. Benefitting from the large exciton binding energy and robust light-
matter interaction of CsPbBr at room temperature27,29,30,34,54,55, we realize such supersolidity at ambient
3
conditions, substantiated by the observation of two thresholds in parametric emission growth behavior, and
coordinate space pattern formation with a period correlated with k position of the parametric polariton.
As illustrated in Fig. 4a, the evolution of intensity exhibits two nonlinear thresholds (marked by black dashed
lines), with sub-linear growth at low pump fluence and subsequent nonlinear growth of source (5.35 μJ cm-
2) and signal/idler (7.44 μJ cm-2), respectively. Different growth behavior of parametric emission with
respect to source BEC density (I) is retrieved by examining the respective intensity evolution closely near
the two thresholds, as shown in Fig. 4b and denoted by I, I0.25, and I0.9. Below the first threshold, incoherent
relaxation from the exciton reservoir, and linear scattering from source polariton is responsible for the
population at signal and idler states. Crossing the first threshold, source condensate first exhibits nonlinear
growth. With source condensate population building up, nonlinear parametric scattering was initiated and
nonlinearly increases the signal and idler intensity, accompanied by a dramatic reorganization in momentum
space as shown in the insets of Fig. 4b. The left inset depicts a uniform exciton reservoir distribution, while
the right inset highlights coherent parametric scattering between the source condensate and conjugate
signal/idler polaritons. Respective angle-resolved PL spectra and momentum space images for this
microcavity at different pump fluences are depicted in Supplementary Fig. 20.

As shown in Fig. 4c–f, for two parametric oscillators with angle-resolved PL spectra (Fig. 4c and e)
showing signal and idler polaritons centered at distinct wavevectors (8.0 μm-1 and 7.2 μm-1), corresponding
features were observed in real space emission patterns. The real space images (Fig. 4d and f, upper panels)
with striking periodic fringes confirm a ‘lattice’ constant of 0.78 μm and 0.87 μm by extracting the line
profiles (lower panels). Such spatial periodicity aligns precisely with the momentum-space emission peaks
via Fourier reciprocity, confirming the spontaneous ‘crystallization’ of the polariton condensate and its
supersolid nature. We believe that such coherent parametric emission with intensity comparable to source
condensate enables direct observation of an anomalous supersolid phase with periodic stripes in real space,
which would otherwise be obscured by strong source condensate emission. In strongly confined
microcavities, such phenomenon with correlated momentum space position and real space fringe spacing
was also observed (Supplementary Fig. 21), except with presence of limited number of fringes due to the
finite dimensionality. Circumventing the extreme cooling requirements of traditional quantum fluids
establishes the optical parametric oscillator in our microcavity as an ideal testbed for emergent macroscopic
quantum effects.

In summary, this work establishes quantum confined semiconductor microcavities as a robust platform for
strong coherent parametric polariton generation through the synergistic interplay of geometric confinement
and surface disorder. Highly efficient parametric emission is achieved in presence of disorder in the strongly
confined regime, with parametric emission intensity rivaling those of the source condensate, while
preserving high spectra-purity with sub-1-meV linewidth. The ultra-narrowband emission enables the
observation of phase coherence between signal and idler polaritons. Statistical analysis from experiments
and theory reveals the role of quantum size effect in mediating parametric emission intensity in the quantum
confined microcavity. In addition, the efficient emission enables direct observation of emerging supersolid
phase at room temperature. These results demonstrate that non-trivial potential landscape act as key
enablers of unconventional parametric phenomena—which could be readily extended to other material
platforms, providing transformation strategies to harness polariton nonlinearities and accelerate the
development of quantum photonic devices.

## Methods

Perovskite Synthesis
The CsPbBr microplatelets were synthesized using an anti-solvent method31. CsBr and PbBr powders of
3 2
analytical grade were mixed in a 1:1 molar ratio and dissolved in dimethylformamide to prepare a 20 mM
precursor solution. Glass substrates were placed in a placed in dichloromethane anti-solvent filled beaker,
and the precursor solution was dropped onto the substrates, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 2a. Beaker was
covered with perforated Parafilm to and placed in an oven with temperature of 30 ℃ for 48 h, enabling
evaporation and CsPbBr single crystal growth. The synthesis procedure yields microplatelets of various
3
lateral dimensions, shown in Supplementary Fig. 2b.

Microcavity Fabrication
The CsPbBr microcavity consists of top and bottom distributed Bragg reflector (DBR) mirrors and the
3
central CsPbBr microplatelets. Bottom DBR consists of 20 pairs of electron-beam evaporated titanium
3
oxide (TiO ) and silicon dioxide (SiO ) with quarter-wavelength thickness, and top DBR consists of 8 pairs
2 2
of such oxide layers. CsPbBr microplatelets were dry transferred to bottom DBR with
3
polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) stamps, followed by ~60 nm PMMA layer encapsulation before top mirror
evaporation, acting as protection layer for perovskites.

Optical Characterization
Optical characterization was conducted using a custom-built system based on Fourier imaging, allowing
for both real-space and momentum-space resolved spectroscopy and imaging. For real space imaging and
spectroscopy on the micron-scale sized sample, a short-focal length lens was used to magnify the image, to
resolve emission from the microplatelet microcavity. A Michelson interferometer with mirror symmetric
configuration was utilized to investigate first-order spatial and temporal coherence in both real space and
k-space. Pump laser spot size was enlarged by a long focal distance lens in the excitation path, as shown in
Supplementary Fig. 6. Emission from the sample was captured with a 100× objective (NA = 0.9) and
spatially filtered with an adjustable rectangular aperture at the focal plane and directed to a liquid nitrogen-
cooled charge-coupled device (CCD) spectrometer (Princeton Instruments, SP-2500i). For pulsed
excitation, the 800 nm fundamental pulses (100 fs, 1 kHz) from a Coherent Astrella regenerative amplifier
were directed to a beta barium borate (BBO) crystal to generate non-resonant pump pulses at 400 nm, or
directed to an optical parametric amplifier (Coherent OperA Solo) to generate resonant pump pulses at 540
nm. Continuous-wave excitation was performed using a 405 nm laser.

Other characterizations
Atomic force microscopy (AFM) imaging was carried out in tapping mode with a BRUKER Dimension
ICON system, while laser confocal microscopy was performed using a Zeiss LSM800 Airyscan confocal
microscope. X-Ray diffraction (XRD) measurement was performed with Rigaku XtaLAB PRO. Annular
dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) characterization was performed with Titan
Cubed Themis G2 at 300 kV voltage. SEM images were obtained from Thermo Fisher Helios G4 UX

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript by Deng et al. reports efficient parametric emission from CsPbBr3 microcavities while preserving a sub 1meV linewidth. The authors claim that the mechanism enabling the highly efficient generation of parametric emission is modulated by quantum confinement. Furthermore, the authors observe spontaneous ‘crystallization’ at room temperature forming a supersolid phase with real space periodicity. The work is relevant to the community, the efficient generation of narrow linewidth parametric emission is a remarkable outcome. However, a deeper analysis of the mechanism enabling this process is essential to make this a scalable process.
Main Comments:
1) The manuscript attributes the discretization of the polariton dispersion to a combination of geometric confinement and disordered surface potentials, with a reported 7.5 meV mode spacing. However, the discussion does not clearly distinguish the contributions from in-plane confinement and disorder. A systematic study isolating the effects of in-plane confinement, and surface roughness, such as comparing dispersions for different lateral sizes and controlled disorder amplitudes, would strengthen the mechanistic interpretation and clarify the origin of the observed discretization. From Fig. 1b, the roughness reaches ~10 nm, an analysis showing that this amplitude can localize lower polaritons and yield a level spacing on the order of the observed, would be beneficial. To separate the two contributions, k-space reflectance for similar cavities with reduced surface roughness would explain how the spacing and the appearance of discrete lines evolve relative to surface roughness.
2) The term “non-confined cavity” needs an explicit definition. A more detailed explanation of what this means would benefit the paper. Does this denote a planar microcavity with a larger crystal? The authors should report the fabrication process for this larger device. Providing these details will allow for a fair comparison with the confined structures.
3) The authors claim that the disordered surface potentials that are formed as a result of the fabrication process are instrumental in generating fine modes and efficient parametric emission. However, the role of the disorder in enhancing parametric emission if not quantitively measured. A study of how the different levels of surface roughness effect the signal /ideler ratio would be beneficial.
4) The authors chose CsPbBr₃ as the active material, but the manuscript does not justify why this particular halide perovskite is uniquely suited for sustaining parametric scattering and supersolid behavior. Could other halide compositions (e.g., CsPbI₃, mixed halides, or hybrid organic-inorganics) offer advantages in terms of exciton binding energy, linewidth, or tunability of the cavity modes? A few sentences in the introduction would help here.
5) The manuscript would benefit from structural characterization of the CsPbBr₃ microplatelets. While the microcavities are strongly characterized, no direct evidence is provided for the crystallographic quality or phase purity of the material. Techniques such as X-ray diffraction could confirm the absence of secondary phases, strain, or structural defects that might influence the dispersion and parametric scattering behavior. Including such data would strengthen the link between the observed effects in the strongly coupled system and the intrinsic properties of the active material, and ensure that the reported effects are not influenced by variations in material quality.
6) Given that perovskites are prone to point defects and surface traps, how do the authors ensure that these do not dominate the coherence and linewidth of the parametric emission? Is there any passivation strategy or post-treatment applied or can you comments on how that might affect properties?

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript “Harnessing highly efficient coherent polariton parametric emission in quantum confined perovskite microcavities” by Xinyi Deng et al. reports the first-time observation of resonantly enhanced parametric scattering of exciton- polaritons in a halide perovskite microcavity. The authors emphasize the key result of their work: the strong influence of in- plane polariton quantization, accompanied by potential disorder, on the nonlinear optical response of the studied system. They experimentally observe coherent polariton emission involving parametric scattering and also claim the “first observation of strong phase coherence between the two parametric species in momentum space.”
The importance of the observations is not in doubt: the suggested arrangement is suitable for generating phase-correlated photon pairs, with potential for operation down to the single-photon regime. The halide perovskite platform is favorable in this sense, as it is known for its ultimate quantum efficiency of exciton-enabled light emission.
The manuscript is generally well-written. However, some further clarifications and polishing of the text would be beneficial, as noted below. The team employs well-established experimental methods; therefore, the data quality is suitable. The analytical model is clear; some parameters used need to be specified in the updated version of the manuscript.
Although I am generally positive about this work, I must point out that some of the authors’ claims require further justification. The authors have to address several questions before I can recommend this work for publication in Nature Communications.
Major issue:
My primary concern is related to the mechanisms of population of signal and idler states. I can suggest at least three of those:
(1) Conventional relaxation from the reservoir to a resonant state (gain).
(2) Linear scattering of polaritons from the source to signal and idler states.
(3) Nonlinear parametric scattering of source polaritons towards signal/idler state, claimed as the primary mechanism.
Firstly, the right panel in Figure 2a clearly shows the strong asymmetry in signal (1.36)/idler (0.43) relative intensities. In case of mechanism (3), exclusively responsible signal/idler population, this picture must be purely symmetric. The largest of these two values is compared to other works in Figure 2b and is referred to as “parametric emission efficiency”, which might mislead the reader. This efficiency is fundamentally limited by the minimum of the two values mentioned for each particular measurement.
The authors state in the text: ”Below the first threshold, incoherent relaxation from the exciton reservoir is responsible for the population at signal and idler states.” It is unclear why authors neglect this mechanism when discussing the system behavior above the first thresholds.
Let me suggest an explanation of the observed effects involving only mechanisms (1) and (2). Above the first threshold, the condensate appears at the source state. The polaritons there undergo elastic scattering into signal/idler modes, with efficiency enhanced by surface disorder. These scattered polaritons seed the condensates in signal/idler states, which appear at a larger threshold and remain coherent with the source, as they are seeded by polaritons coming from it. Another reason for the signal, source, and idler states to be mutually coherent is the complete overlap of these modes in real space.
The condensation threshold for the signal/idler states can be larger than that of the source state for several reasons, including differences in polariton lifetimes. The nearest polaritonic state below the source is more than 50 meV apart, while for signal/idler states, this distance is below 10 meV.
I firmly believe that with this massive amount of experimental data in hand, authors can distinguish between mechanisms (1- 3) more accurately.
Another way to completely exclude the mechanism (1) from the list is to perform additional measurements with the resonant pumping of the source state by appropriately tuning the excitation photon energy and adjusting the spot size to avoid direct excitation of signal/indler modes. To distinguish pump photons from those in a condensate (and estimate the condensate emission rate), one can pump at an angle, staying within the positive/negative in-plane wavevectors, yet remaining resonant with the source mode.
Additional related question: What are the values of net gains P_n for signal, source, and idler used for the modelling in Figure S11?
Minor remarks:
1. In the manuscript, only the elastic scattering process is discussed. Meanwhile, Figure 2c reveals an apparent spectral mismatch between signal, source, and indler emission peaks. Owing to the inversion symmetry of the system, is there any explanation for this effect? Could it be a measurement artifact, such as a slight misalignment of the CCD camera, which needs to be corrected during data post-processing?
2. In the text, the authors compare confined and unconfined microcavities. Unfortunately, I was unable to find the two respective definitions. It is worth clarifying this for the reader.
3. I suggest adding a discussion on the role of the second dimension of the rectangular microcavities. Why can the confinement in the second dimension be neglected?
4. I was also unable to find an explicit discussion of the role of potential disorder. How does surface roughness improve the system's performance?
One aspect could be as follows. Polariton, scattering on surface roughness, may acquire an additional portion of momentum, inversely proportional to the lateral size of the surface feature. This process, therefore, enhances scattering from the source to signal/idler states.
5. Authors state: “Meanwhile, downscaling the confinement dimension leads to energy eigenstates with larger spacing that induces the randomness in matching of source and signal/idler energy position, leading to a larger fluctuation amplitude in parametric interaction strength and acquisition of highly efficient parametric emission in confined microcavities.”
Indeed, the LA1 and LA2 branches have generally different sets of quantized levels. The detuning (and overlap) between the fundamental level of LA1 (the source state) and the nearest LA2 state is expected to significantly affect both linear and nonlinear elastic scattering processes in the system.
In this context, would the data presented in red symbols in Figure 3a, showing nearly random behavior, become better structured when used to correlate signal&idler/source with the LA1-LA2 nearest-level detuning? Of course, the randomness induced by surface roughness will stand.
6. Within the text, one can find many terms, probably referring to the exact property of the system under study: surface potential landscape, disorder potential landscape, disordered surface potential landscape, transfer-induced potential landscape, disorder potential, etc. I recommend leaving a single term.
7. The authors should proofread the Supplementary Material:
Figure S2 ( “microscope” misspelled),
Figure S5 (d-f) - is it a single frequency or summation over a range?
Figure S6 (b) and (a) should be exchanged.
Figure S7 (g) instead of (b). It is unclear why the source and idler energy- and wavevector-dependent spectra are plotted on different axes. I suggest using the exact representation and adding the signal plots as well.
I would be glad to review the revised manuscript if the authors address the concerns and questions that have been raised.
